verses.zh: 耶稣进了耶利哥，正经过的时候，
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] entered Jericho[NOTE:2] and was passing through it.
notes: Grk “And entering, he passed through”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
For location see Map5-B2; Map6-E1; Map7-E1; Map8-E3; Map10-A2; Map11-A1.

verses.zh: 有一个人名叫撒该，作税吏长，是个财主。
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] a man named Zacchaeus was there; he was a chief tax collector[NOTE:2] and was rich.
notes: Grk “And behold.” Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the introduction of a new character. The Greek word ἰδού (idou) at the beginning of this statement has not been translated because it has no exact English equivalent here, but adds interest and emphasis (BDAG 468 s.v. 1).

This is the one place in the NT the office of chief tax collector is noted. If the term refers to a managerial rank, this individual would organize and oversee the other tax collectors and collect significant commissions (see also the note on the word tax collector in 3:12). It is possible, however, that in this context the term simply means “major tax collector” and is a comment on the individual’s importance or wealth rather than his rank (see D. L. Bock, Luke [BECNT] 1:1516).

verses.zh: 他要看看耶稣是怎样的人；只因人多，他的身量又矮，所以不得看见，
verses.en: He[NOTE:1] was trying to get a look at Jesus,[NOTE:2] but being a short man he could not see over the crowd.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “He was trying to see who Jesus was.”
Grk “and he was not able to because of the crowd, for he was short in stature.”

verses.zh: 就跑到前头，爬上桑树，要看耶稣，因为耶稣必从那里经过。
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] he ran on ahead and climbed up into a sycamore tree[NOTE:2] to see him because Jesus[NOTE:3] was going to pass that way.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of Zacchaeus not being able to see over the crowd.
A sycamore tree would have large branches near the ground like an oak tree and would be fairly easy to climb. These trees reach a height of some 50 ft (about 15 m).
Grk “that one”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 耶稣到了那里，抬头一看，对他说：「撒该，快下来！今天我必住在你家里。」
verses.en: And when Jesus came to that place, he looked up[NOTE:1] and said to him, “Zacchaeus, come down quickly[NOTE:2] because I must[NOTE:3] stay at your house today.”[NOTE:4]
notes: Most mss (A [D] W [Ψ] ƒ13 33vid M latt) read “Jesus looking up, saw him and said.” The words “saw him and” are not in א B L T Θ ƒ1 579 1241 2542 co. Both the testimony for the omission and the natural tendency toward scribal expansion argue for the shorter reading here.
Grk “hastening, come down.” σπεύσας (speusas) has been translated as a participle of manner.
I must stay. Jesus revealed the necessity of his associating with people like Zacchaeus (5:31-32). This act of fellowship indicated acceptance.
On today here and in v. 9, see the note on today in 2:11.

verses.zh: 他就急忙下来，欢欢喜喜地接待耶稣。
verses.en: So he came down quickly[NOTE:1] and welcomed Jesus[NOTE:2] joyfully.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “hastening, he came down.” σπεύσας (speusas) has been translated as a participle of manner.
Grk “him”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

The participle χαίρων (chairōn) has been taken as indicating manner.sn Zacchaeus responded joyfully. Luke likes to mention joy as a response to what God was doing (1:14; 2:10; 10:20; 13:17; 15:5, 32; 19:37; 24:41, 52).

verses.zh: 众人看见，都私下议论说：「他竟到罪人家里去住宿。」
verses.en: And when the people[NOTE:1] saw it, they all complained,[NOTE:2] “He has gone in to be the guest of a man who is a sinner.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “they”; the referent is unspecified but is probably the crowd in general, who would have no great love for a man like Zacchaeus who had enriched himself many times over at their expense.

This term is used only twice in the NT, both times in Luke (here and 15:2) and has negative connotations both times (BDAG 227 s.v. διαγογγύζω). The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Being the guest of a man who is a sinner was a common complaint about Jesus: Luke 5:31-32; 7:37-50; 15:1-2.

verses.zh: 撒该站着对主说：「主啊，我把所有的一半给穷人；我若讹诈了谁，就还他四倍。」
verses.en: But Zacchaeus stopped and said to the Lord, “Look, Lord, half of my possessions I now give[NOTE:1] to the poor, and if[NOTE:2] I have cheated anyone of anything, I am paying back four times as much!”
notes: Zacchaeus was a penitent man who resolved on the spot to act differently in the face of Jesus’ acceptance of him. In resolving to give half his possessions to the poor, Zacchaeus was not defending himself against the crowd’s charges and claiming to be righteous. Rather as a result of this meeting with Jesus, he was a changed individual. So Jesus could speak of salvation coming that day (v. 9) and of the lost being saved (v. 10).
This is a first class condition in the Greek text. It virtually confesses fraud.

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「今天救恩到了这家，因为他也是亚伯拉罕的子孙。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus said to him, “Today salvation[NOTE:2] has come to this household[NOTE:3] because he too is a son of Abraham![NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative
This is one of the few uses of the specific term salvation in Luke (1:69, 71, 77), though the concept runs throughout the Gospel.
The household is not a reference to the building, but to the people who lived within it (L&N 10.8).
Zacchaeus was personally affirmed by Jesus as a descendant (son) of Abraham and a member of God’s family.

verses.zh: 人子来，为要寻找、拯救失丧的人。」
verses.en: For the Son of Man came[NOTE:1] to seek and to save the lost.”
notes: The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost is Jesus’ mission succinctly defined. See Luke 15:1-32.

verses.zh: 众人正在听见这些话的时候，耶稣因为将近耶路撒冷，又因他们以为　神的国快要显出来，就另设一个比喻，说：
verses.en: While the people were listening to these things, Jesus[NOTE:1] proceeded to tell a parable because he was near to Jerusalem,[NOTE:2] and because they thought[NOTE:3] that the kingdom of God[NOTE:4] was going to[NOTE:5] appear immediately.
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
The present active infinitive δοκεῖν (dokein) has been translated as causal.
Luke means here the appearance of the full kingdom of God in power with the Son of Man as judge as Luke 17:22-37 describes.
Or perhaps, “the kingdom of God must appear immediately (see L&N 71.36).

verses.zh: 「有一个贵胄往远方去，要得国回来，
verses.en: Therefore he said, “A nobleman[NOTE:1] went to a distant country to receive[NOTE:2] for himself a kingdom and then return.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “a man of noble birth” or “a man of noble status” (L&N 87.27).

Note that the receiving of the kingdom takes place in the far country. This suggests that those in the far country recognize and acknowledge the king when his own citizens did not want him as king (v. 14; cf. John 1:11-12).

The background to this story about the nobleman who went…to receive for himself a kingdom had some parallels in the area’s recent history: Archelaus was appointed ethnarch of Judea, Samaria, and Idumea in 4 b.c., but the people did not like him. Herod the Great also made a similar journey to Rome where he was crowned King of Judea in 40 b.c., although he was not able to claim his kingdom until 37 b.c.

verses.zh: 便叫了他的十个仆人来，交给他们十锭（锭：原文是弥拿，一弥拿约银十两）银子，说：『你们去做生意，直等我回来。』
verses.en: And he summoned ten of his slaves,[NOTE:1] gave them ten minas,[NOTE:2] and said to them, ‘Do business with these until I come back.’
notes: See the note on the word “slave” in 7:2.
That is, one for each. A mina was a Greek monetary unit worth 100 denarii or about four months’ wages for an average worker based on a six-day work week.

verses.zh: 他本国的人却恨他，打发使者随后去，说：『我们不愿意这个人作我们的王。』
verses.en: But his citizens[NOTE:1] hated[NOTE:2] him and sent a delegation after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man[NOTE:3] to be king[NOTE:4] over us!’
notes: Or “subjects.” Technically these people were not his subjects yet, but would be upon his return. They were citizens of his country who opposed his appointment as their king; later the newly-appointed king will refer to them as his “enemies” (v. 27).
The imperfect is intense in this context, suggesting an ongoing attitude.
Grk “this one” (somewhat derogatory in this context).
Or “to rule.”

verses.zh: 他既得国回来，就吩咐叫那领银子的仆人来，要知道他们做生意赚了多少。
verses.en: When[NOTE:1] he returned after receiving the kingdom, he summoned[NOTE:2] these slaves to whom he had given the money. He wanted[NOTE:3] to know how much they had earned[NOTE:4] by trading.
notes: Grk “And it happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.
Grk “he said for these slaves to be called to him.” The passive construction has been translated as an active one and simplified to “he summoned.”

Grk “in order that he might know” (a continuation of the preceding sentence). Due to the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the pronoun “he” as subject and the verb “wanted” to convey the idea of purpose.
The Greek verb earned refers to profit from engaging in commerce and trade (L&N 57.195). This is an examination of stewardship.

verses.zh: 头一个上来，说：『主啊，你的一锭银子已经赚了十锭。』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the first one came before him and said, ‘Sir,[NOTE:2] your mina[NOTE:3] has made ten minas more.’
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the royal summons.
Or “Lord”; or “Master.” (and so throughout this paragraph).
See the note on the word “minas” in v. 13.

verses.zh: 主人说：『好！良善的仆人，你既在最小的事上有忠心，可以有权柄管十座城。』
verses.en: And the king[NOTE:1] said to him, ‘Well done, good slave! Because you have been faithful[NOTE:2] in a very small matter, you will have authority[NOTE:3] over ten cities.’
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
See Luke 16:10.
The faithful slave received expanded responsibility (authority over ten cities) as a result of his faithfulness; this in turn is an exhortation to faithfulness for the reader.

verses.zh: 第二个来，说：『主啊，你的一锭银子已经赚了五锭。』
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] the second one came and said, ‘Sir, your mina has made five minas.’
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.

verses.zh: 主人说：『你也可以管五座城。』
verses.en: So[NOTE:1] the king[NOTE:2] said to him, ‘And you are to be over five cities.’
notes: Here δέ (de) has been translated as “so” to indicate the implied result of the second slave’s report.
Grk “he”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 又有一个来说：『主啊，看哪，你的一锭银子在这里，我把它包在手巾里存着。
verses.en: Then another[NOTE:1] slave[NOTE:2] came and said, ‘Sir, here is[NOTE:3] your mina that I put away for safekeeping[NOTE:4] in a piece of cloth.[NOTE:5]
notes: Though ten were given minas, the story stops to focus on the one who did nothing with the opportunity given to him. Here is the parable’s warning about the one who does not trust the master. This figure is called “another,” marking him out as different than the first two.
The word “slave” is not in the Greek text, but has been supplied for stylistic reasons.
Grk “behold.”
Or “that I stored away.” L&N 85.53 defines ἀπόκειμαι (apokeimai) here as “to put something away for safekeeping—‘to store, to put away in a safe place.’”
The piece of cloth, called a σουδάριον (soudarion), could have been a towel, napkin, handkerchief, or face cloth (L&N 6.159).

verses.zh: 我原是怕你，因为你是严厉的人；没有放下的，还要去拿，没有种下的，还要去收。』
verses.en: For I was afraid of you because you are a severe[NOTE:1] man. You withdraw[NOTE:2] what you did not deposit[NOTE:3] and reap what you did not sow.’
notes: Or “exacting,” “harsh,” “hard.”

Grk “man, taking out.” The Greek word can refer to withdrawing money from a bank (L&N 57.218), and in this context of financial accountability that is the most probable meaning. Because of the length and complexity of the Greek sentence, a new sentence was started here in the translation by supplying the pronoun “you” as subject and translating the participle αἴρεις (aireis) as a finite verb.
The Greek verb τίθημι (tithēmi) can be used of depositing money with a banker to earn interest (L&N 57.217). In effect the slave charges that the master takes what he has not earned.

verses.zh: 主人对他说：『你这恶仆，我要凭你的口定你的罪。你既知道我是严厉的人，没有放下的，还要去拿，没有种下的，还要去收，
verses.en: The king[NOTE:1] said to him, ‘I will judge you by your own words,[NOTE:2] you wicked slave![NOTE:3] So you knew, did you, that I was a severe[NOTE:4] man, withdrawing what I didn’t deposit and reaping what I didn’t sow?
notes: Grk “He”; the referent (the nobleman of v. 12, now a king) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Grk “out of your own mouth” (an idiom).
Note the contrast between this slave, described as “wicked,” and the slave in v. 17, described as “good.”
Or “exacting,” “harsh,” “hard.”

verses.zh: 为甚么不把我的银子交给银行，等我来的时候，连本带利都可以要回来呢？』
verses.en: Why then didn’t you put[NOTE:1] my money in the bank,[NOTE:2] so that when I returned I could have collected it with interest?’
notes: That is, “If you really feared me why did you not do a minimum to get what I asked for?”
Grk “on the table”; the idiom refers to a place where money is kept or managed, or credit is established, thus “bank” (L&N 57.215).

verses.zh: 就对旁边站着的人说：『夺过他这一锭来，给那有十锭的。』
verses.en: And he said to his attendants,[NOTE:1] ‘Take the mina from him, and give it to the one who has ten.’[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “to those standing by,” but in this context involving an audience before the king to give an accounting, these would not be casual bystanders but courtiers or attendants.
Grk “the ten minas.”

verses.zh: 他们说：『主啊，他已经有十锭了。』
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] they said to him, ‘Sir, he has ten minas already!’[NOTE:2]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context. Those watching the evaluation are shocked, as the one with the most gets even more. The word “already” is supplied at the end of the statement to indicate this surprise and shock.
A few mss (D W 69 and a few versional witnesses) omit this verse either to harmonize it with Matt 25:28-29 or to keep the king’s speech seamless.

verses.zh: 主人说：『我告诉你们，凡有的，还要加给他；没有的，连他所有的也要夺过来。
verses.en: ‘I tell you that everyone who has will be given more,[NOTE:1] but from the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away.[NOTE:2]
notes: Grk “to everyone who has, he will be given more.” sn Everyone who has will be given more. Again, faithfulness yields great reward (see Luke 8:18; also Matt 13:12; Mark 4:25).

The one who has nothing has even what he seems to have taken away from him, ending up with no reward at all (see also Luke 8:18). The exact force of this is left ambiguous, but there is no comfort here for those who are pictured by the third slave as being totally unmoved by the master. Though not an outright enemy, there is no relationship to the master either. Three groups are represented in the parable: the faithful of various sorts (vv. 16, 18); the unfaithful who associate with Jesus but do not trust him (v. 21); and the enemies (v. 27).

verses.zh: 至于我那些仇敌，不要我作他们王的，把他们拉来，在我面前杀了吧！』」
verses.en: But as for these enemies of mine who did not want me to be their king,[NOTE:1] bring them here and slaughter[NOTE:2] them[NOTE:3] in front of me!’”
notes: Grk “to rule over them.”
This term, when used of people rather than animals, has some connotations of violence and mercilessness (L&N 20.72).
Slaughter them. To reject the king is to face certain judgment from him.

verses.zh: 耶稣说完了这话，就在前面走，上耶路撒冷去。
verses.en: After Jesus[NOTE:1] had said this, he continued on ahead,[NOTE:2] going up to Jerusalem.[NOTE:3]
notes: Grk “he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
This could mean “before [his disciples],” but that is slightly more awkward, requiring an elided element (the disciples) to be supplied.

For location see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.sn This is yet another travel note on the journey to Jerusalem. See also Luke 18:31; 19:11. Jesus does not actually enter Jerusalem until 19:45.

verses.zh: 将近伯法其和伯大尼，在一座山名叫橄榄山那里，就打发两个门徒，说：
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] when he approached Bethphage[NOTE:2] and Bethany, at the place called the Mount of Olives,[NOTE:3] he sent two of the disciples,
notes: Grk “And it happened that when.” The introductory phrase ἐγένετο (egeneto, “it happened that”), common in Luke (69 times) and Acts (54 times), is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated. Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
The exact location of the village of Bethphage is not known. Most locate it on the southeast side of the Mount of Olives and northwest of Bethany, about 1.5 miles (3 km) east of Jerusalem.

Grk “at the mountain called ‘of Olives.’” This form of reference is awkward in contemporary English, so the more familiar “Mount of Olives” has been used in the translation.sn “Mountain” in English generally denotes a higher elevation than it often does in reference to places in Palestine. The Mount of Olives is really a ridge running north to south about 1.8 mi (3 km) long, east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley. Its central elevation is about 100 ft (30 m) higher than Jerusalem. It was named for the large number of olive trees which grew on it.

verses.zh: 「你们往对面村子里去，进去的时候，必看见一匹驴驹拴在那里，是从来没有人骑过的，可以解开牵来。
verses.en: telling them,[NOTE:1] “Go to the village ahead of you.[NOTE:2] When[NOTE:3] you enter it, you will find a colt tied there that has never been ridden.[NOTE:4] Untie it and bring it here.
notes: Grk “saying.”
Grk “the village lying before [you]” (BDAG 530 s.v. κατέναντι 2.a).
Grk “in which entering.” This is a continuation of the previous sentence in Greek, but because of the length and complexity of the construction a new sentence was started here in the translation.
Grk “a colt tied there on which no one of men has ever sat.”

verses.zh: 若有人问为甚么解它，你们就说：『主要用它。』」
verses.en: If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ just say, ‘The Lord needs[NOTE:1] it.’”
notes: The custom called angaria allowed the impressment of animals for service to a significant figure.

verses.zh: 打发的人去了，所遇见的正如耶稣所说的。
verses.en: So those who were sent ahead found[NOTE:1] it exactly[NOTE:2] as he had told them.
notes: Grk “sent ahead and went and found.”
Exactly as he had told them. Nothing in Luke 19-23 catches Jesus by surprise. Often he directs the action.

verses.zh: 他们解驴驹的时候，主人问他们说：「解驴驹做甚么？」
verses.en: As[NOTE:1] they were untying the colt, its owners asked them,[NOTE:2] “Why are you untying that colt?”
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “said to them.”

verses.zh: 他们说：「主要用它。」
verses.en: They replied, “The Lord needs it.”

verses.zh: 他们牵到耶稣那里，把自己的衣服搭在上面，扶着耶稣骑上。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] they brought it to Jesus, threw their cloaks[NOTE:2] on the colt,[NOTE:3] and had Jesus get on[NOTE:4] it.
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “garments,” but this refers in context to their outer cloaks. The action is like 2 Kgs 9:13.
See Zech 9:9.

Although ἐπεβίβασαν (epebibasan) is frequently translated “set [Jesus] on it” or “put [Jesus] on it,” when used of a riding animal the verb can mean “to cause to mount” (L&N 15.98); thus here “had Jesus get on it.” The degree of assistance is not specified.

verses.zh: 走的时候，众人把衣服铺在路上。
verses.en: As[NOTE:1] he rode along, they[NOTE:2] spread their cloaks on the road.
notes: Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.

The disciples initiated this action (since in 19:35 and 37 they are the subject) but the other gospels indicate the crowds also became involved. Thus it is difficult to specify the referent here as “the disciples” or “people.”

verses.zh: 将近耶路撒冷，正下橄榄山的时候，众门徒因所见过的一切异能，都欢乐起来，大声赞美　神，
verses.en: As he approached the road leading down from[NOTE:1] the Mount of Olives,[NOTE:2] the whole crowd of his[NOTE:3] disciples began to rejoice[NOTE:4] and praise[NOTE:5] God with a loud voice for all the mighty works[NOTE:6] they had seen:[NOTE:7]
notes: Grk “the descent of”; this could refer to either the slope of the hillside itself or the path leading down from it (the second option has been adopted for the translation, see L&N 15.109).
See the note on the name Mount of Olives in v. 29.
Grk “the”; the Greek article has been translated here as a possessive pronoun (ExSyn 215).
Here the participle χαίροντες (chairontes) has been translated as a finite verb in English; it could also be translated adverbially as a participle of manner: “began to praise God joyfully.”
Or “works of power,” “miracles.” Jesus’ ministry of miracles is what has drawn attention. See Luke 7:22.
Grk “they had seen, saying.” The participle λέγοντες (legontes) is redundant in contemporary English and has not been translated.

verses.zh: 说：奉主名来的王是应当称颂的！在天上有和平；在至高之处有荣光。
verses.en: “Blessed is the king[NOTE:1] who comes in the name of the Lord![NOTE:2] Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”
notes: Luke adds the title king to the citation from Ps 118:26 to make clear who was meant (see Luke 18:38). The psalm was used in looking for the deliverance of the end, thus leading to the Pharisees’ reaction.
A quotation from Ps 118:26.

verses.zh: 众人中有几个法利赛人对耶稣说：「夫子，责备你的门徒吧！」
verses.en: But[NOTE:1] some of the Pharisees[NOTE:2] in the crowd said to him, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples.”[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context. Not all present are willing to join in the acclamation.
See the note on Pharisees in 5:17.
Teacher, rebuke your disciples. The Pharisees were complaining that the claims were too great.

verses.zh: 耶稣说：「我告诉你们，若是他们闭口不说，这些石头必要呼叫起来。」
verses.en: He answered,[NOTE:1] “I tell you, if they[NOTE:2] keep silent, the very stones[NOTE:3] will cry out!”
notes: Grk “and answering, he said.” This has been simplified in the translation to “He answered.” Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “these.”
This statement amounts to a rebuke. The idiom of creation speaking means that even creation knows what is taking place, yet the Pharisees miss it. On this idiom, see Gen 4:10 and Hab 2:11.

verses.zh: 耶稣快到耶路撒冷，看见城，就为它哀哭，
verses.en: Now[NOTE:1] when Jesus[NOTE:2] approached[NOTE:3] and saw the city, he wept over it,
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “now” to indicate the transition to a new topic.
Grk “he.”
When Jesus approached and saw the city. This is the last travel note in Luke’s account (the so-called Jerusalem journey), as Jesus approached and saw the city before entering it.

verses.zh: 说：「巴不得你在这日子知道关系你平安的事；无奈这事现在是隐藏的，叫你的眼看不出来。
verses.en: saying, “If you had only known on this day,[NOTE:1] even you, the things that make for peace![NOTE:2] But now they are hidden[NOTE:3] from your eyes.
notes: On this day. They had missed the time of Messiah’s coming; see v. 44.
Grk “the things toward peace.” This expression seems to mean “the things that would ‘lead to,’ ‘bring about,’ or ‘make for’ peace.”

But now they are hidden from your eyes. This becomes an oracle of doom in the classic OT sense; see Luke 13:31-35; 11:49-51; Jer 9:2; 13:7; 14:7. They are now blind and under judgment (Jer 15:5; Ps 122:6).

verses.zh: 因为日子将到，你的仇敌必筑起土垒，周围环绕你，四面困住你，
verses.en: For the days will come upon you when your enemies will build[NOTE:1] an embankment[NOTE:2] against you and surround you and close in on you from every side.
notes: Jesus now predicted the events that would be fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in a.d. 70. The details of the siege have led some to see Luke writing this after Jerusalem’s fall, but the language of the verse is like God’s exilic judgment for covenant unfaithfulness (Hab 2:8; Jer 6:6, 14; 8:13-22; 9:1; Ezek 4:2; 26:8; Isa 29:1-4). Specific details are lacking and the procedures described (build an embankment against you) were standard Roman military tactics.
An embankment refers to either wooden barricades or earthworks, or a combination of the two.

verses.zh: 并要扫灭你和你里头的儿女，连一块石头也不留在石头上，因你不知道眷顾你的时候。」
verses.en: They will demolish you[NOTE:1]—you and your children within your walls[NOTE:2]—and they will not leave within you one stone[NOTE:3] on top of another[NOTE:4] because you did not recognize the time of your visitation from God.”[NOTE:5]
notes: Grk “They will raze you to the ground.” sn The singular pronoun you refers to the city of Jerusalem personified.
Grk “your children within you.” The phrase “[your] walls” has been supplied in the translation to clarify that the city of Jerusalem, metaphorically pictured as an individual, is spoken of here.
(Not) one stone on top of another is an idiom for total destruction.
Grk “leave stone on stone.”

You did not recognize the time of your visitation refers to the time God came to visit them. They had missed the Messiah; see Luke 1:68-79.tn Grk “the time of your visitation.” To clarify what this refers to, the words “from God” are supplied at the end of the verse, although they do not occur in the Greek text.

verses.zh: 耶稣进了殿，赶出里头做买卖的人，
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] Jesus[NOTE:2] entered the temple courts[NOTE:3] and began to drive out those who were selling things there,[NOTE:4]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “then” to indicate the implied sequence of events within the narrative.
Grk “he.”
The merchants (those who were selling things there) would have been located in the Court of the Gentiles.tn Grk “the temple” (also in v. 47).

Matthew (21:12-27), Mark (11:15-19) and Luke (here, 19:45-46) record this incident of the temple cleansing at the end of Jesus’ ministry. John (2:13-16) records a cleansing of the temple at the beginning of Jesus’ ministry. See the note on the word temple courts in John 2:14 for a discussion of the relationship of these accounts to one another.

verses.zh: 对他们说：「经上说：我的殿必作祷告的殿，你们倒使它成为贼窝了。」
verses.en: saying to them, “It is written, ‘My house will be a house of prayer,’[NOTE:1] but you have turned it into a den[NOTE:2] of robbers!”[NOTE:3]
notes: A quotation from Isa 56:7.
Or “a hideout” (see L&N 1.57).

A quotation from Jer 7:11. The meaning of Jesus’ statement about making the temple courts a den of robbers probably operates here at two levels. Not only were the religious leaders robbing the people financially, but because of this they had also robbed them spiritually by stealing from them the opportunity to come to know God genuinely. It is possible that these merchants had recently been moved to this location for convenience.

verses.zh: 耶稣天天在殿里教训人。祭司长和文士与百姓的尊长都想要杀他，
verses.en: Jesus[NOTE:1] was teaching daily in the temple courts. The chief priests and the experts in the law[NOTE:2] and the prominent leaders among the people were seeking to assassinate[NOTE:3] him,
notes: Grk “And he”; the referent (Jesus) has been specified in the translation for clarity. Here καί (kai) has not been translated because of differences between Greek and English style.
Grk “and the scribes.” See the note on the phrase “experts in the law” in 5:21.

Grk “to destroy.”sn The action at the temple was the last straw. In their view, if Jesus could cause trouble in the holy place, then he must be stopped, so the leaders were seeking to assassinate him.

verses.zh: 但寻不出法子来，因为百姓都侧耳听他。
verses.en: but[NOTE:1] they could not find a way to do it,[NOTE:2] for all the people hung on his words.[NOTE:3]
notes: Here καί (kai) has been translated as “but” to indicate the contrast present in this context.
Grk “they did not find the thing that they might do.”
All the people hung on his words is an idiom for intent, eager listening. Jesus’ popularity and support made it unwise for the leadership to seize him.
